title: More German than many Germans
author: mertbio
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: In 2017, after I finished the third year of my Computer Science studies, I decided to do an internship in Europe. So while I was applying for the Erasmus Scholarship, I also started looking for internships. In the end I got the scholarship, which helped a lot with the visa process, and I also found an internship at a company in Hamburg.I had never been outside of Turkey before. So I had also never really talked to people from other countries. What I knew about Germans came mostly from the Turkish people who moved to Germany in the 60s for work. Those people came back to Turkey almost every summer and told us about their life there. Most of what they said was the same as what you can read on the internet, the stereotypical German.People who don't laugh, who are cold and unfriendly, who always follow the rules, who speak a language that sounds too harsh, and so on. And of course, someone always brings up the Nazis.Apart from the people I talked to in the interviews, my first real contact was my German flatmate. Before I arrived he showed me the room on Skype and we agreed on it. When I landed in Hamburg, he picked me up from the airport. That was a great start, and during my three months there we chatted in the kitchen almost every evening for half an hour.I had a lot of questions for him and he always answered them properly. On the weekends he picked up his girlfriend and they either stayed home or went rowing. Their relationship looked very healthy to me. She was studying medicine, so sometimes she was working at her desk on a Saturday while my flatmate played Witcher 3 right next to her. I never heard them argue about anything.Near the end of my internship he told me that he and his girlfriend were going to Africa, so I would be alone in the flat for a week. When I asked him what I should do with the keys, he just said to drop them in the mailbox. That much trust after such a short time really surprised me.We had a last dinner together and I told him things were going well at the company and there was a chance I could come back to Hamburg.I was lucky with my flatmate and I was also lucky at work. I had a great team. They taught me new things, gave me responsibilities the other summer interns didn't get, and included me in all the team events. The offsite we had outside the city is something I still remember today. And I was getting all of this while earning minimum wage.My first offsite eventI was really surprised by how friendly everyone was. We weren't just working, we were having fun. Everything I had heard about Germans until that point was gone. It was the best summer of my life.My lead was happy with my work and offered me a job right away. I could work as a freelancer from Turkey while finishing my studies, and if they were happy with my performance I would get a full-time contract. That is what happened.Coming backIn April 2018 I got my contract, even before I finished my studies. The next month something nice happened. My German flatmate emailed me and asked when I was coming back, because he already had a room for me for the summer. The company was going to give me a place to stay, but I couldn't say no to him. Right after my last exam, before I even had my diploma, I moved to Hamburg at the end of June and started working full time with the same team, living with the same flatmate.On my first day there were candies and balloons on my desk. Everybody was happy to see me again. One colleague who knew my interest in Apple gave me a German flag pin he got at WWDC18. He said he tried to swap it for a Turkish flag but couldn't manage it. I was already happy with the gift, because it meant he was thinking about me while he was in California.My deskWhen you start living in Germany you have to register your address. When I went to the public office, the clerk told me I had already lived in Hamburg before. I said I had done a summer internship a year earlier. He just said: Welcome back!That was the moment I felt like I was coming home, not moving to a new country.The first yearsMy first months were mostly about finding a flat and figuring out how things work here. Since my German wasn't good enough, my colleagues came with me to flat viewings after work. When I had a problem with my electricity provider, a colleague came along and did all the talking. When I moved to a different place a year later, a German colleague rented a van and helped me carry everything.At the time, the company was one of the biggest internet companies here, with around 2.000 people. Sometimes I saw the C-level in the kitchen getting their own coffee or even washing their own glasses. They had assistants, but the assistants helped with work instead of acting like servants. We also had a CFO who rode a very old bike to the office.Whenever we had a team event or an offsite, the organisers made sure they knew everyone's dietary needs. Vegan, vegetarian, halal, no alcohol, allergies. So everyone would have something to eat and drink.When I was doing a good job, my lead kept telling me to take vacation instead of working more. When I was sick, he told me to stay home until I felt better. I didn't even need a doctor's note. It took me a while to notice this was not only a work thing. You get on a bus or a train here and nobody checks your ticket. I wasn't used to this level of trust.My second offsiteAcross from our office there was an Italian restaurant where we went for pizza sometimes. The pizzas were very tasty and huge, and it was the only place that sold half a pizza. At lunch I saw people in suits eating there, and right at the next table people from the construction site nearby in their work clothes eating the same pizza. Nobody looked at the other table and nobody thought it was worth noticing except me. That is the part that stayed with me. It was completely normal, and it was normal because a man who spent his morning on a building site can afford an Italian lunch and eat it like everyone else.I noticed the same thing in the rich districts of Hamburg. You can walk into one and not feel like you don't belong, and the prices in the shops are not that different from anywhere else in the city. Sometimes they are exactly the same. The more I saw of that, the more I wanted to stay. I believe in social democracy, and this is a country that calls itself one and mostly behaves like it.It didn't take long for me to move up at work. I didn't feel any discrimination, even though people say Germans prefer Germans when it comes to promotions. There were already a lot of people with a migration background at the top. When I ran as a candidate in the works council election, I got the most votes of anyone, even though there were many Germans running and only around 25% of the company were immigrants like me.You see the same thing outside of companies. Cem Özdemir, whose parents came from Turkey, has been the prime minister of Baden-Württemberg since May. Sinan Selen, who was born in Istanbul, runs the office for the protection of the constitution.Being in the works council gave me more contact with the C-level. Sometimes I found myself arguing with the CTO or the CEO, and later at a company party we would have a beer together and talk about something else. That is when I understood how flat the management is here. I saw the difference later when I worked for an American company, where they made sure you knew you were lower on the ladder.I met hundreds of Germans at that company and they were always super friendly. I say this because years later I still see many of my old colleagues at different events, and most of my friends today are people I used to work with. A lot of immigrants complain that it is hard to become friends with Germans, but that wasn't my experience.My landing was softI should be honest about one thing here. I landed softly. I came into a big international company where everyone spoke English, in a city like Hamburg, with a salary that let me pick where I live. I have worked with other German companies since then, mostly smaller ones, so what I write here is not only about that one place. But the start was much easier for me than it is for most people. A lot of them arrive with none of that, and the country they meet is not the same one I met. Everything I write here is my experience, not a report on how it works for everyone.The language is part of that. Every story I told above happened in English. The team, the flatmate, the works council, the arguments with the CEO, all of it. Once I decided I was going to stay here for a long time, I started taking German classes, and after the citizenship law changed I put much more effort into it. So the German came from the decision to stay. It was not the thing that made me stay.I never really tried to integrate. It just happened that the way I think about life turned out to be similar to how people here think.Why I like the rulesMost people complain about the rules in Germany, but I like them. It means someone, or a group of people, sat down and thought about that specific thing and decided on a standard for everyone. When you have to do something, you don't feel lost, because you can just look it up. You don't have to find someone who knows.Rules also make normal days easier. Something simple like waiting at a red light even when there are no cars takes away the work of deciding whether to cross. And if everyone does it, you don't have to worry about someone suddenly stepping into the street. Or the fire safety rule that makes exit doors in public buildings open outwards. You never have to think about pull or push.There are also unwritten rules, like being on time. For me the logical thing has always been to aim for 15 minutes before the agreed time, so if something happens on the way I'm still fine. After going on dates with a lot of Germans, I realised they do the same thing. So instead of me arriving early and waiting 15 minutes, we just meet 15 minutes earlier.My favourite one is Ruhezeit, the quiet time between 10PM and 6AM, plus Sundays and public holidays. My sleep is very important to me and I'm a light sleeper, so this rule really helps me. Sometimes I had neighbours who had parties during those hours, and I didn't hesitate to complain (with Lärmprotokoll) to my landlord. Many Germans have told me I'm more German than many Germans. It is probably because of examples like this one.The one time a rule was pointed at me instead of working for me was my first application for permanent residence. I had just left my first company and I was between jobs, and that was enough to get it rejected. That was when I learned what a sustainable livelihood means to the German authorities. It doesn't mean the money you have in your account. It means a permanent contract with the probation time already behind you. I had savings and it didn't count for anything.It was an emotional day. But after I calmed down I could see their logic. A bank balance can be gone in a year and a signed contract that already survived six months says something a number can't. It was the same system I like for every other reason, just this time I was on the wrong side of it.Understanding the countryThe longer I lived here, the more I saw myself spending the rest of my life here. That made me want to read about the country. I'm a heavy reader and I track every book, so here are the ones I read about Germany:German Men Sit Down To Pee & Other Insights Into German CultureGermany: Memories of a NationThe German GeniusKaput: The End of the German MiracleMan's Search for MeaningBlood and Iron: The Rise and Fall of the German Empire 1871 to 1918Why the Germans Do it Better: Notes from a Grown-Up CountryApart from the books, I also watched a lot of documentaries, especially about the Nazi era.Like most people, I didn't know that Germany wasn't one country until the 19th century. It was made of small kingdoms, city states and so on. That is why there are so many kinds of bread, beer and sausage, why some parts have different public holidays, different accents and even a different way of living.The German Genius surprised me the most. It is about 1.000 pages about Germans who contributed to humanity in different fields, and I didn't know how many things in our daily life exist thanks to them. Some of them had to escape the country because of the Nazis and reached their full potential somewhere else, in countries like the US and the UK. The books also helped me understand how Germany built an educated middle class, how workers' rights and social reforms happened, and where the rule about no shopping on Sundays comes from.What stayed with me is that this is probably the only country in the western world that faced its own history properly, admitted the worst things it did, and built a lot of its identity around not repeating them. You feel that here in small ways, not only in museums. In January 2024, after it came out that far right politicians had talked about deporting people who already hold a German passport, 50.000 to 80.000 people filled the streets of my city in one afternoon."Hamburg steht auf!" demonstrationIn eight years I have not had a single case of racism. I know that isn't true for everyone, and I know the far right keeps growing.I don't think most of those votes are about hating foreigners. Some people believe the story they get every day, that the country is broken and that immigrants are the problem. You find that story almost everywhere. The rest are angry that certain problems here have not been solved for years by the existing parties, so they look for an alternative.For me, Germans are people who give trust before it is earned. People who are friendly without being fake about it. People who make sure everyone is included, down to what is on the table. People who care about someone they will never meet. People who know exactly what happened here and don't look away from it.Making it officialThat is why I decided to become one of them.The chance came when the traffic light coalition, which I think was the most progressive government this country has had in decades, changed the citizenship rules and brought the waiting time down to five years. I was eligible, so I applied.People seem to think a German passport is handed out easily now. It isn't. You have to prove you paid into the social system for at least five years. You have to pass the citizenship test. You need German at B1 level. You need a sustainable livelihood while your application is running. And most importantly, you have to accept the democratic values of this country.For me the process itself was smooth. I applied online by uploading a pile of PDFs. A week later I got a letter saying my application had arrived, with a few papers to sign, scan and upload back. Then the waiting started. In total it took around 14 months to get the email saying my application was successful and that I could come and collect my Einbürgerungsurkunde.I picked it up this week, at an appointment that only took 15 minutes. I am German now.I believe I have contributed something to this society in these eight years and I will keep doing it. And I will keep complaining about everything that needs to be better. Because that is what real Germans do.
No spam, no sharing to third party. Only you and me.

comments.author: rockyj
comments.textRawHtml:
A very nice read and pretty much my experience. I have been here for a quarter of my life now, I do not think I can live anywhere else now. People may not like me being here because of my skin color or whatever but I do not mind. I keep to myself and follow all the "rules" I can. In fact, I like most of the rules, rules are good because they ensure order, fairness and equality.

Will a little bit of empathy be nicer, sure, but I cannot complain. Speaking of which, a lot of German natives complain and some are even leaving the country (around 100k left last year), but honestly I have visited / lived in nine countries, and people have no idea how good they have it here. I came here with a bag, twenty euros in my pocket and a job offer, a dozen years later I have pretty much all basic comforts and stability one can dream of, my kids have a bright future waiting for them, all this is not possible in many countries.
comments.textZhHtml:
非常好的读物和我的经历。我已经在这里度过了四分之一的人生，我想我现在不能住在其他地方了。人们可能因为我的肤色或其他什么原因不喜欢我在这里，但我不介意。我保持自我并遵守所有我能遵守的“规则”。其实我喜欢大部分的规则，规则是好的，因为它保证了秩序、公平和平等。

当然，有一点同理心会更好，但我不能抱怨。说到这里，很多德国人都在抱怨，有些人甚至要离开这个国家（去年还剩下10万左右），但老实说，我已经访问/居住过九个国家，人们不知道他们在这里过得有多好。我带着一个包来到这里，口袋里有二十欧元和一份工作机会，十几年后我几乎拥有了人们可以梦想的所有基本舒适和稳定，我的孩子们有一个光明的未来在等待着他们，这一切在许多国家都是不可能的。

children.author: wuschel
children.textRawHtml:
> Speaking of which, a lot of German natives complain and some are even leaving the country (around 100k left last year), but honestly I have visited / lived in nine countries, and people have no idea how good they have it here.

The grass is always greener on the other side ... until you actually dare to find out. Having lived and worked in many a country, I second your opinion that it is often about trade offs. Problems will come and go. You have to choose the problem you want to work with.

Germany certainly is one of the top countries to live in.
children.textZhHtml:
> 说到这里，很多德国人都在抱怨，有些人甚至要离开这个国家（去年还剩下10万左右），但老实说，我已经访问/居住过九个国家，人们不知道他们在这里过得有多好。

彼岸的草总是更绿……直到你真正敢于发现。我在许多国家生活和工作过，我同意你的观点，即这通常与权衡有关。问题会来来去去。你必须选择你想要解决的问题。

德国无疑是最适宜居住的国家之一。

children.author: ido
children.textRawHtml:
My opinion (immigrant for the 2nd time, currently in Germany since 2013- so I've lived in 3 countries when counting my native one):

Basically, all rich/"western" countries are pretty decent. Some better than other, but they're all 'ok' or rather they all have plenty of 'ok' options for people able to work at somewhat in-demands fields (despite the financial situation of the last couple years a career in tech or tech adjacent generally still fits that category).

If you go somewhere where there's "real" problems, countries like Egypt, India, Ethiopia (altho of course there are nice areas in these countries too) you realize most of the time you'd rather live in any rich country than in a poor country. And there are more people worldwide living in countries ± like India than in countries ± like Germany.
children.textZhHtml:
我的看法（第二次移民，自 2013 年以来目前在德国 - 所以算上我的祖国，我已经在 3 个国家生活过）：

基本上，所有富裕/“西方”国家都相当不错。有些比其他更好，但它们都“还可以”，或者更确切地说，它们都为那些能够在一些有需求的领域工作的人提供了很多“还可以”的选择（尽管过去几年的财务状况，技术或邻近技术的职业通常仍然适合这一类别）。

如果你去的地方有“真实的“问题是，像埃及、印度、埃塞俄比亚这样的国家（当然这些国家也有不错的地区）你意识到大多数时候你宁愿居住在 任何 富裕国家比贫穷国家好。全世界生活在印度这样的国家的人比生活在德国这样的国家的人还要多。

children.author: piva00
children.textRawHtml:
> If you like how a country does things, why not change the country you originate from instead of going to that other country?

Because it's neigh impossible for an individual to meaningfully change parts of the culture they dislike which are ingrained for hundreds of years.

How am I supposed to change one of the major issues plaguing my home country: corruption? It's ingrained at all levels, from politicians to the police, and people participate in it because it's simply the way it is. By rejecting corruption I just made my life harder at all levels, it took me months longer to fix tax issues because I didn't want to pay someone who knew someone and could have it fixed in a matter of days; registering my car at the time took a whole week of visiting different offices, paying government fees in-person at banks so I could get receipts officially stamped, ordering a plate was a 2-day endeavour, I could have paid a person who would have fixed everything in a day but that involves being part of corruption so I rejected it.

I cannot change that, it's part of the culture, it annoyed me to no end, and my individual actions didn't matter at all while making my life harder.

It was much better for my life to emigrate, and live at a place where society is fundamentally more aligned to my values and ways of living.
children.textZhHtml:
> 如果你喜欢一个国家的做事方式，为什么不改变你的原籍国而不是去另一个国家呢？

因为一个人几乎不可能有意义地改变他们不喜欢的文化中根深蒂固数百年的部分。

我该如何改变困扰我祖国的主要问题之一：腐败？它在从政治家到警察的各个层面都根深蒂固，人们参与其中，因为它就是这样。通过拒绝腐败，我只是让我在各个层面的生活变得更加困难，我花了几个月的时间来解决税务问题，因为我不想付钱给认识某人并且可以在几天内解决问题的人；当时登记我的车花了整整一个星期的时间，走访了不同的办公室，亲自去银行支付政府费用，这样我就可以得到正式盖章的收据，订购车牌需要两天的时间，我本来可以付钱给一个人，他可以在一天内解决所有问题，但这涉及腐败，所以我拒绝了。

我无法改变这一点，这是文化的一部分，它让我无休止地烦恼，我的个人行为根本无关紧要，同时让我的生活变得更加困难。

移民到一个社会从根本上更符合我的价值观和生活方式的地方，对我的生活来说要好得多。

children.author: breppp
children.textRawHtml:
> I cannot change that, it's part of the culture, it annoyed me to no end, and my individual actions didn't matter at all while making my life harder.

That's never true, countries changed extremely, also cultural-wise. If talking Germany the basic example is changing from a very militaristic society (far before the Nazis) to a rather pacifist society.

If talking corruption, my own country has progressively became far less corrupt over my lifetime
children.textZhHtml:
> 我无法改变这一点，这是文化的一部分，它让我无休无止地烦恼，我的个人行为根本无关紧要，同时让我的生活变得更加困难。

这从来都不是真的，国家和文化方面都发生了巨大的变化。如果谈论德国，基本的例子就是从一个非常军国主义的社会（远远早于纳粹）转变为一个相当和平主义的社会。

如果谈论腐败，我自己的国家在我一生中已经逐渐变得不那么腐败了

children.author: piva00
children.textRawHtml:
> That's never true, countries changed extremely, also cultural-wise. If talking Germany the basic example is changing from a very militaristic society (far before the Nazis) to a rather pacifist society.

After suffering a massive defeat, losing millions of lives, and being occupied for decades.

Otherwise culture changes slowly, I won't waste my lifetime to see 5-10% improvements, you are totally free to move to Brazil and fix it for us since it seems to be an easy task for you.

> If talking corruption, my own country has progressively became far less corrupt over my lifetime

In mine it only got worse, religious nuts like Evangelicals only accumulated more power over my life there, in my almost 30 years living there progress outside of economical terms got stuck.

Corruption is only one issue, violence is another major one, macho-culture and sexism is yet another, religiousness in the form of Evangelicalism with tele-pastors only grew to become >50% of the population.

It's an absolute fantasy that me staying there for my next 30-50 years of life would've made any difference. I only have one life, I won't waste it at a place where I always felt like a fish out of water with no power to change it. My life won't be dedicated to politics and power plays to the point where I could have any meaningful impact, I'm just a normal person trying to live a decent life, not an agent of change, lol.

You are completely invited to move there and change it though.
children.textZhHtml:
> 这从来都不是真的，国家和文化方面都发生了巨大的变化。如果谈论德国，基本的例子就是从一个非常军国主义的社会（远远早于纳粹）转变为一个相当和平主义的社会。

在遭受了巨大的失败、数百万人丧生、被占领数十年之后。

否则文化会慢慢改变，我不会浪费我的一生来看到 5-10% 的改进，你完全可以自由地搬到巴西并为我们修复它，因为这对你来说似乎是一件容易的任务。

> 如果谈论腐败，我自己的国家在我一生中已经逐渐变得不那么腐败了

在我那里，情况只会变得更糟，像福音派这样的宗教狂热分子只会在我在那里的生活中积累更多的权力，在我在那里生活的近 30 年里，经济方面以外的进步陷入了困境。

腐败只是一个问题，暴力是另一个主要问题，大男子主义文化和性别歧视是另一个问题，福音派形式的宗教信仰和远程牧师只会增长到超过人口的 50%。

如果我在接下来的 30 到 50 年里留在那里，会对我的生活产生任何影响，这绝对是一种幻想。我的生命只有一次，我不会把它浪费在一个我总是感觉像鱼离开水而无力改变它的地方。我的生活不会致力于政治和权力游戏，以至于我可以产生任何有意义的影响，我只是一个试图过上体面生活的普通人，而不是变革的推动者，哈哈。

不过，我们完全邀请您搬到那里并进行更改。

children.author: lbschenkel
children.textRawHtml: Hear hear, from another Brazilian (now dual citizen) who emigrated.
children.textZhHtml: 听听另一位移民的巴西人（现在是双重公民）的说法。

children.author: a2800276
children.textRawHtml:
> If talking Germany the basic example is changing from a very militaristic society (far before the Nazis) to a rather pacifist society.

I seem to recall that this was not the result of Germans staying put and changing things for the better, but rather due to external forces reducing the majority of their country to rumble and and spending 2 decades reeducating them.

Not sure what "your country" is, but here in Germany that's the general consensus of Germany's progression to a "rather" pacifist society. You might want to take pacifist with a grain of salt though, considering how excited many Germans were about being able to deploy the Army for non defensive reasons in the Balkans, Afghanistan, etc. and how giddy everyone was that we were once again allowed to export arms to Ukraine. Not to mention the current rise of far right, xenophobic parties.

Fighting corruption is very difficult. A good way to go about it is to sent some of your young people to countries that don't have massive problems in order come back home viscerally convinced it's not a necessary evil you need to put up with.
children.textZhHtml:
> 如果谈论德国，基本的例子就是从一个非常军国主义的社会（远远早于纳粹）转变为一个相当和平的社会。

我似乎记得，这并不是德国人原地踏步并让事情变得更好的结果，而是由于外部力量使他们国家的大部分地区陷入混乱，并花了 20 年的时间对他们进行再教育。

不确定什么是“你的国家”，但在德国这里这是德国向“相当”和平主义社会发展的普遍共识。不过，考虑到许多德国人对于能够出于非防御原因在巴尔干、阿富汗等地部署陆军感到多么兴奋，以及每个人对于我们再次被允许向乌克兰出口武器感到多么兴奋，你可能会对和平主义者持保留态度。更不用说目前极右翼仇外政党的崛起。

打击腐败非常困难。 一个好办法就是把一些年轻人送到没有严重问题的国家，然后回国时发自内心地相信这不是你需要忍受的必然罪恶。

children.author: aleph_minus_one
children.textRawHtml:
> considering how excited many Germans were about being able to deploy the Army for non defensive reasons in the Balkans, Afghanistan, etc.

Having lived at that time in Germany, I can tell you how excited many Germans rather were to openly name the responsible politicians "war criminals" (and would have been insanely happy if these politicians were brought before a war crimes tribunal) and the compatriot soldiers to participated in this campaign "murderers". I know this very well because I was among these people.

Even on the schoolyard there was a deep divide between the boys who were not completely rejecting the idea to do their (at that time near-compulsory) military service instead of considering at most doing alternative service as the only acceptable alternative, and those who did alternative service did then use every available opportunity to spread their opinion about wars and the military (they often had to work their alternative service in some welfare facility or retirement homes - places where you meet lots of people to whom you could tell your "soldiers are murderers" opinions).
children.textZhHtml:
> 考虑到许多德国人对能够出于非防御原因在巴尔干地区、阿富汗等地部署军队感到多么兴奋。

当时生活在德国，我可以告诉你，许多德国人对于公开称负责任的政客为“战犯”（如果这些政客被带到战争罪行法庭的话会非常高兴）和参加这场战役的同胞士兵感到多么兴奋“杀人犯”。我很清楚这一点，因为我就是这些人中的一员。

即使在校园里，男孩们之间也存在着深刻的分歧，他们并没有完全拒绝服兵役（当时几乎是强制性的）兵役，而最多只考虑参加替代性服役作为唯一可接受的选择，而那些参加替代性服役的男孩则利用一切可用的机会来传播他们对战争和军队的看法（他们经常不得不在一些福利机构或养老院中从事替代性服役——在这些地方你会遇到很多人）你可以告诉他们你的“士兵是杀人犯”的观点）。

children.author: breppp
children.textRawHtml:
The way I see it is the cultural change happened after the Prussian elites lost power and the general German public understood their recent history as far from the eternal victory they were promised. That's a major cultural change however you want to spin it, and there are enough examples in history where countries haven't gone through the same changes in similar situations (Weimar Republic also comes to mind)

Regarding the current day pacifist state of Germany, in my mind it is still very drastic anti-militaristic compared to the vast majority of the world.

Regarding corruption, countries changed drastically during the 20th century due to ideologies and individual action, sometimes resulting in disaster but also often not. Trying to say nothing can change is a defeatist deterministic attitude that has no anchor in recent history.

Presuming we are talking about migration, most of these source countries were able to fight and win European colonization in the past, why do you think that's easier than fighting corruption?
children.textZhHtml:
我认为，文化变革是在普鲁士精英失去权力之后发生的，德国公众对他们最近的历史的理解与他们所承诺的永恒胜利相去甚远。无论你想怎么解释，这都是一次重大的文化变革，历史上有足够多的例子表明，一些国家在类似情况下没有经历过同样的变化（魏玛共和国也浮现在我的脑海中）

关于德国当今的和平主义国家，在我看来，与世界上绝大多数国家相比，它仍然是非常激烈的反军国主义。

关于腐败，由于意识形态和个人行动，国家在 20 世纪发生了巨大变化，有时会导致灾难，但也常常不会。试图说没有什么可以改变是一种失败主义的决定论态度，在近代历史中没有立足点。

假设我们谈论的是移民，这些来源国大多数过去都能够抗击并赢得欧洲殖民统治，为什么你认为这比打击腐败更容易？

children.author: a2800276
children.textRawHtml:
> Presuming we are talking about migration, most of these source countries were able to fight and win European colonization in the past, why do you think that's easier than fighting corruption?

While I neither claimed "nothing can change" corruption nor that fighting corruption is more difficult than fighting European colonization, here are some arguments to your straw man:

Corruption is very insidious to combat because you don't have a clearly demarcated enemy to unite against. Corruption spreads through all layers of society and most people in deeply corrupt societies will be both victims and beneficiaries of corruption: you want your house built and saved up enough dough? Sure you grease the wheels a bit so you can start building right away. Also, your brother who's helping you finance the house is a civil servant and a good chunk of his income is a result of taking bribes. The government itself sees it as "tips" that justify lower wages, and you sure as shit don't want taxes to go up with all the baksheesh you need to hand out...

At best you're in a "glass house" scenarios, it's very difficult to break out of without a general amnesty and serious external pressure, because all the parties that are actually qualified to run a government (or similar corrupt organization) are implicated.
children.textZhHtml:
> 假设我们正在谈论移民，大多数这些来源国过去都能够抗击并赢得欧洲殖民化，为什么你认为这比打击腐败更容易？

虽然我既没有声称“没有什么可以改变”腐败，也没有声称打击腐败比打击欧洲殖民化更困难，但这里有一些对你的稻草人的论据：

腐败是非常阴险的，因为你没有一个明确划分的界限团结起来对抗的敌人。腐败蔓延到社会各阶层，腐败严重的社会中的大多数人既是腐败的受害者，又是腐败的受益者：你想建好房子并攒够钱吗？当然，你已经给轮子涂了一点润滑油，这样你就可以立即开始建造了。另外，帮你买房的兄弟是一名公务员，他的收入很大一部分来自受贿。政府本身将其视为证明低工资合理的“小费”，而且你肯定不希望税收随着你需要发放的所有baksheesh而上涨......

充其量你处于“玻璃屋”情景中，如果没有普遍的特赦和严重的外部压力，很难摆脱困境，因为所有实际上有资格管理政府（或类似腐败组织）的各方都受到牵连。

children.author: breppp
children.textRawHtml:
Yes, and the founding belief of corruption is that, "that's the way it works", "everybody does it", "this can never change".

That essentialism is exactly the notion the poster I was replying to was echoing

Western countries were also corrupt at a time, bribery was common, yet things can change
children.textZhHtml:
是的，腐败的基本信念是“事情就是这样”、“每个人都这样做”、“这永远不会改变”。

这种本质主义正是我回复的发帖者所呼应的观念

西方国家也曾一度腐败，贿赂很常见，但事情是可以改变的

children.author: a2800276

But the "Prussian elites lost power" because of the rise of the National Socialists who are universally not considered pacifist.

It might be a "major cultural change" but it was not affected by people staying at home and changing things for the better.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我认为文化变革是在普鲁士精英失去权力之后发生的，而德国公众对他们最近的历史的理解与他们所承诺的永恒胜利相去甚远。

但是“普鲁士精英失去权力”是因为普遍不被认为是和平主义者的国家社会主义者的崛起。

这可能是一个“重大文化变革”，但它并没有受到人们呆在家里并为国家而改变事物的影响。更好。

children.author: abcd_f
children.textRawHtml: One will be long dead when a desired fundamental change finally completes. So any suggestion to stay and wait it out is plain disingenuous.
children.textZhHtml: 当期望的根本性改变最终完成时，一个人就会死去很久。因此，任何留下来等待事情结束的建议都是不诚实的。

children.author: breppp
children.textRawHtml:
Why? Do you think a country is going to improve if anyone with potential like the OP would move to the West?

I haven't suggested someone should wait it out, but the notion that nothing can ever change because it's "culture" sounds absurd to me and as an excuse to not try
children.textZhHtml:
为什么？如果像OP这样有潜力的人会搬到西方，你认为一个国家会进步吗？

我并没有建议人们应该等待，但因为它是“文化”而什么都不会改变的观念对我来说听起来很荒谬，并且作为不尝试的借口

children.author: piva00
children.textRawHtml:
> I haven't suggested someone should wait it out, but the notion that nothing can ever change because it's "culture" sounds absurd to me and as an excuse to not try

I simply did not want to waste more of time by feeling powerless, I spent 10 years in civics organisations from 18-28 which didn't effect any change whatsoever even though we organised protests, education outreach for people to understand how government systems worked at each level for more conscious voting, one of my closest friends is a constitutional lawyer and helped to write motions to the state assembly.

Nothing of that ever helped anything, I wasted 10 years participating in civics for absolutely no gain. Much the contrary, I've been beaten by police, tear gas'ed, had a rubber bullet shot on my thigh (with a visible mark still there, 15 years later).

At some point you run out of steam, you are more than welcome to pick up the fight I gave up though.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我并没有建议有人应该等待它结束，但是因为它是“文化”而没有任何东西可以改变的想法对我来说听起来很荒谬，并且作为不尝试的借口

我只是不想浪费更多时间感到无能为力，我从18岁到28岁在公民组织中度过了10年，尽管我们组织了抗议活动，但没有影响任何变化，教育外展让人们了解政府系统如何运作在每个级别上为了更有意识的投票，我最亲密的朋友之一是一名宪法律师，他帮助向州议会撰写动议。

这些都没有任何帮助，我浪费了 10 年时间参与公民活动，却毫无收获。恰恰相反，我被警察殴打，被催泪弹击中，大腿上被橡皮子弹射中（15 年后，痕迹仍然清晰可见）。

在某些时候，你会失去动力，但我们非常欢迎你继续我放弃的战斗。

children.author: kmijyiyxfbklao
children.textRawHtml: You are supposed to fixed the same way the first world countries fixed it, by staying there are improving things with the other people that want to improve things. Oh wait they all left for other countries, oops I guess people that couldn't leave get to stay and rot in unfixable corruption.
children.textZhHtml: 你应该像第一世界国家那样解决问题，通过留在那里与其他想要改善事情的人一起改善事情。哦，等等，他们都去了其他国家，哎呀，我猜那些无法离开的人会留下来，在无法修复的腐败中腐烂。

children.author: piva00
children.textRawHtml:
That's what happens when a culture is broken to the point of requiring generations of work to fix it: people who are unhappy will leave because there's no hope for enough to change to keep them there.

How do you imagine that me staying in Brazil would have helped fixing major issues with corruption and violence? It's my life, I won't waste it living in a fantasy that as an individual I will have any meaningful impact on lowering corruption, homicides, robberies, so on and so forth.

I'm just a person trying to live a good life, my home country didn't provide it while I tried to live with my values, I decided to move on and had the privilege to be able to do so, of course I will take it.
children.textZhHtml:
当一种文化被破坏到需要几代人的努力来修复它时，就会发生这种情况：不满意的人会离开，因为没有希望做出足够的改变来留住他们。

您认为我留在巴西会如何帮助解决腐败和暴力等重大问题？这是我的生命，我不会浪费它生活在幻想中，作为一个个体，我将对减少腐败、凶杀、抢劫等等产生任何有意义的影响。

我只是一个试图过上美好生活的人，我的祖国没有提供它，而我试图按照我的价值观生活，我决定继续前进，并有幸能够这样做，我当然会接受它。

children.author: aleph_minus_one
children.textRawHtml:
> I won't waste it living in a fantasy that as an individual I will have any meaningful impact on lowering corruption, homicides, robberies, so on and so forth.

The difference is: Some people are willing incredibly hard to fight for this, even though it is obvious to them that they will have no meaningful impact. Shouldn't you rather be willing to fight magnitudes harder if you know that you will have no meaningful impact because:

- Realizing that you will have no meaningful impact rather makes you realize how important the fight is.

- When you know that you won't have any chance of a meaningful impact, you will much less held back by having any kind of mercy with any person that is part of the corrupt system.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我不会把时间浪费在幻想中，以为作为个人，我将对减少腐败、凶杀、抢劫等产生任何有意义的影响。

区别在于：有些人愿意为此付出难以置信的努力，尽管这对他们来说是显而易见的它们不会产生任何有意义的影响。如果你知道自己不会产生任何有意义的影响，你难道不应该愿意更加努力地战斗吗？因为：

- 意识到你不会产生任何有意义的影响，反而会让你意识到战斗多么重要。

- 当你知道你不会有任何机会产生有意义的影响时，你就不会因为对腐败体系中的任何人有任何仁慈而退缩。
